chapterTitle: Broken Authentication, Session Management, and Access Control
aiGenerationNote: Create a 15-minute live demo video. Begin by demonstrating a simple brute-force attack on a vulnerable login form using Burp Suite Intruder, highlighting weak password policies. Then, transition to an IDOR exploitation scenario on a DVWA-like application, showing how to change `id` parameters in the URL and in Burp Repeater to access unauthorized user data. Finally, illustrate a session hijacking scenario by manually manipulating a `PHPSESSID` cookie in browser developer tools to impersonate another user. Use clear terminal and browser views, with Burp Suite prominently displayed. Emphasize the importance of server-side validation and strong session management. Include a "Common Mistakes" overlay about relying on client-side security.

screens.title: Broken Authentication, Session Management, and Access Control
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we will examine how applications fail to verify identity, maintain session state, and enforce authorization. You will learn what broken authentication means in practice: weak passwords, predictable recovery tokens, and missing multi-factor defenses. We will then explore session weaknesses like hijacking and fixation, where an attacker reuses or forces a session identifier to impersonate a user. Finally, we will study broken access control, including vertical escalation, horizontal escalation, and insecure direct object references. Each idea is tied to concrete testing techniques using tools you already know, such as Burp Suite and simple browser dev tools. Through hands-on steps you will practice changing URL parameters, manipulating cookies, and replaying modified requests to confirm whether the server enforces authorization. Why this matters: authentication and access control are often the gateway to all other vulnerabilities. A single predictable token or an exposed session value can let an attacker reach privileged data or actions. As you proceed, notice common misconceptions: client-side controls are not protections and obfuscation does not equal authorization. Keep an eye out for concrete mitigations we will demonstrate: cryptographically random tokens, HttpOnly and Secure cookies, session rotation, and server-side ownership checks. By the end you should be able to detect these flaws, exploit them in a lab safely, and recommend effective fixes. What is one small change that could stop the simplest attacks you see here?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Broken Authentication, Session Management, and Access Control

Explore practical failure modes where identity and authorization checks break down. Learn hands-on techniques to detect, exploit, and fix them in lab environments such as DVWA and Juice Shop.

Core problems visualized
Authentication, sessions, and access control are connected. A single weakness can cascade into full takeover.
Authentication
Weak passwords, reset tokens
Sessions
Hijackable or fixed IDs
Access Control
IDOR, privilege escalation
Impact
Data exposure or admin takeover
Explore Key Topics
Authentication
How identity checks and password recovery can fail and how to harden them.
Session Management
Why session tokens must be random, secure, and rotated after login.
Access Control
Server-side authorization, IDOR, and privilege boundaries to prevent escalation.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide practical skills you will build. First, you will identify common authentication weaknesses such as weak password policies, predictable reset tokens, and missing multi-factor authentication. That means you will learn to recognize how poor design invites brute-force and credential stuffing. Second, you will understand session management attacks including session hijacking and fixation. You will be able to explain why long, random tokens and cookie flags like HttpOnly and Secure matter. Third, you will explain broken access control categories: vertical and horizontal privilege escalation and IDOR. You will be able to categorize findings and describe the missing server-side checks. Fourth, you will demonstrate exploitation techniques safely in a lab using tools such as Burp Suite, applying Repeater and Intruder to validate flaws. Each objective pairs with a verification milestone so you can show evidence of competency, such as a captured modified request proving an IDOR or a rotated session ID after login. Misconception to avoid: observing a disabled button or hidden link on the client is not proof of authorization. Server-side checks are the ultimate gate. Keep these goals in mind as you follow the hands-on activity and mitigation patterns.

screens.title: Practical and testing objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on tools, testing habits, and common pitfalls. You will learn to use Burp Suite Repeater and Intruder to validate authentication and access control issues safely. That includes intercepting requests, modifying parameters like user identifiers, and replaying altered requests to confirm whether the server grants unauthorized access. Second, you will practice safe lab setup: use DVWA or Juice Shop inside an isolated environment and never test production systems. Third, you will learn to articulate mitigation recommendations: enforce strong, unique reset tokens, enable multi-factor authentication, apply HttpOnly and Secure cookie flags, and rotate session IDs after login. Fourth, you will be able to document findings with proof, such as a modified request showing an IDOR or a cookie change that results in admin access. A common misconception to watch for is assuming obfuscated parameters or client-side checks are secure. The verification milestone is simple: reproduce the flaw in the lab and describe the exact missing server-side validation that allowed it. These objectives ensure you not only find flaws but also explain precise fixes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Testing Objectives

Practical and testing objectives

What you must be able to do in a lab and how to report it responsibly.

Use Burp Repeater & Intruder
Intercept, modify, and replay requests to validate IDOR and authentication weaknesses. Repeater proves authorization gaps; Intruder helps test password strength at scale.
Safe lab setup
Run DVWA or Juice Shop in an isolated environment and avoid testing live production systems to prevent unintended harm.
Document proof
Capture modified requests and responses that demonstrate the missing server-side checks needed to reproduce the issue.
Recommend fixes
Propose server-side mitigations like random tokens, MFA, secure cookie flags, session rotation, and authorization checks per resource.

screens.title: What is Broken Authentication?
screens.narratorSegment: Broken authentication means the application does not reliably verify who is trying to access an account or resource. Common examples include weak password policies that accept short or common passwords, insufficient protection against credential stuffing where attackers reuse leaked usernames and passwords, and predictable password reset tokens that can be guessed. A concrete example from a test environment: if password reset links use sequential integers as tokens, an attacker can enumerate or brute-force tokens to reset other users' passwords. Another weakness is informative error messages that reveal whether a username exists, enabling user enumeration. When you test a login form, tools such as Burp Suite Intruder can automate credential lists against the form to confirm weak policies or missing account lockout. A key misconception is believing that client-side validation prevents attacks; it does not. Attackers interact with the server directly. The defending approach includes enforcing long, complex passwords or rate limiting, enabling multi-factor authentication, and using single-use, cryptographically random reset tokens with short expiry. Finally, ensure account lockouts are implemented correctly and cannot be trivially bypassed. Takeaway: authentication must be treated as a critical control point and designed to resist automated and targeted abuse. How would you prove a reset token is predictable in a lab?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Broken authentication occurs when identity verification mechanisms are weak, predictable, or bypassable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Broken Authentication

What is Broken Authentication?

Flaws that allow attackers to assume another user's identity or bypass login protections.

Detailed definition
  • Weak password policies enable brute-force and credential stuffing.
  • Predictable or sequential reset tokens allow unauthorized resets.
  • Verbose errors enable username enumeration.
  • MFA absence converts a leaked password into full account access.
Concrete example
If a reset endpoint returns token values like token=1, token=2, an attacker can iterate values until a valid reset link works.
Testing pattern
# Example manual test with Burp
# 1. Request a reset for a known user
# 2. Capture the reset link and note the token
# 3. Increment the token value and request the link
# 4. Observe whether other tokens succeed
Key Takeaway

Treat reset tokens as secrets: make them long, random, single-use, and short-lived.

screens.title: Session Management Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Session management is the mechanism that preserves a user's identity across multiple stateless HTTP requests. A server issues a session token after successful authentication and the client presents it on subsequent requests to maintain access. The correct process includes generating a long, cryptographically secure token, setting cookie attributes like HttpOnly and Secure, using SameSite when appropriate, rotating the token on privilege change or login, and invalidating it on logout or timeout. Session hijacking happens when an attacker obtains an existing valid token and reuses it to impersonate the user. Examples include tokens sent over plain HTTP or tokens that are predictable. Session fixation is different: an attacker forces—or convinces—the victim to use a specific token, then waits for the victim to authenticate; if the server does not issue a new token upon authentication, the attacker already owns that session. Misconception: clearing cookies in the browser proves the server invalidated the session; it does not. Always verify server-side invalidation. Practical checks: observe Set-Cookie headers in responses, change the cookie value manually and load the site to confirm access, and verify that tokens change after login. Protect sessions by rotating IDs after login and enforcing short idle timeouts. How would you demonstrate session fixation in a lab?

keyIdea.title: Session claims
keyIdea.text: Sessions must use unpredictable tokens, secure cookie flags, rotation on login, and server-side invalidation to prevent hijack and fixation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Session Management

Session Management Fundamentals

Understand the lifecycle of a session token and the attacks that abuse it.

Session lifecycle
  1. 1. Authenticate -> server creates a long random token.
  2. 2. Server sets cookie with Secure and HttpOnly flags.
  3. 3. Token presented on each request to prove identity.
  4. 4. On logout or idle timeout the server invalidates the token.
Common mistakes
Using sequential or predictable IDs, not rotating the token after login, and relying on client-side deletion as proof of invalidation.
Practical checks
- Inspect Set-Cookie headers and token values.
- Manually change cookie values and reload to test hijack.
- Confirm token rotation after authentication or privilege change.
Pro tip

Always run tests in an isolated lab and record the exact token and request that proved access, for reproducible evidence.

screens.title: Testing IDOR: Modify and Replay
screens.narratorSegment: Insecure Direct Object References, or IDORs, occur when an application uses user-supplied identifiers to access objects without checking whether the requester is authorized. The core test is simple: capture a request where a user views a resource and modify the identifier to another value to see if the server returns a different user's data. A practical walkthrough uses a DVWA-like environment and Burp Suite Repeater. First, find a request that includes a parameter such as id=1. Send it to Repeater. Change id to 2 and resend. If the server returns user two's profile, the server is trusting the parameter without authorization checks. A common misconception is that obfuscating the id on the client prevents access; it does not because an attacker works directly with the HTTP layer. Example evidence includes two response bodies showing different user details for id=1 and id=2. When documenting, capture both requests and responses and note the missing server-side check: there was no ownership or role verification for the requested resource. Mitigation involves server-side mapping from authenticated user to authorized objects and rejecting requests where the requested object is not owned or permitted. How would you show that client-side obfuscation was bypassed?

keyIdea.title: IDOR test
keyIdea.text: Modify object identifiers in intercepted requests and replay them to verify whether access is authorized by the server.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Testing IDOR

Testing IDOR: Modify and Replay

Capture a resource request, change the object id, and resend to check for unauthorized access.

Manual Repeater steps
GET /vulnerabilities/idor/?id=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: dvwa
Cookie: PHPSESSID=abcd1234

# Modify to id=2 and resend
GET /vulnerabilities/idor/?id=2 HTTP/1.1
Host: dvwa
Cookie: PHPSESSID=abcd1234
If the second response contains the other user's profile, the server lacks authorization checks and an IDOR exists.
Evidence to capture
  • Both requests with the modified parameter.
  • Both responses showing different users' data.
  • Note of server behavior when id is invalid or missing.
Common mistake

Relying on client-side obfuscation or hidden fields to protect IDs. Always verify server-side checks.

screens.title: Exploiting Session Hijacking via Cookie Manipulation
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson guides a controlled lab exercise that demonstrates session hijacking by manipulating a session cookie. The lab uses DVWA with Burp Suite configured as a proxy. First, log in as the admin user and find the login response with Set-Cookie containing PHPSESSID or another session token. Record that token from Burp HTTP history. Next, log out and log in as a different low-privileged user and capture that session token as well. To prove hijack, open a fresh browser profile or clear cookies, then manually set the cookie for the DVWA domain to the admin session value you recorded. Reload the site; if the server accepts that session value, you will be logged in as admin without credentials. This demonstrates why tokens must be resistant to theft and why secure transport and token invalidation matter. Misconception: simply seeing a cookie value in the browser means the server validated its origin; the server must reject forged or expired tokens. Mitigations include sending cookies only over HTTPS, setting HttpOnly to prevent script access, and rotating or invalidating tokens after logout. When you report this finding, include the original captured Set-Cookie header and the reproduction steps so reviewers can confirm the issue reliably.

keyIdea.title: Session hijacking lab
keyIdea.text: Capture a session token in a proxy, set it manually in a fresh browser, and observe if the server accepts the session to demonstrate hijackability.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Session Hijacking Lab

Exploiting Session Hijacking via Cookie Manipulation

Follow these steps in an isolated lab to demonstrate cookie-based session takeover.

Step-by-step checklist
  1. 1. Log in as admin and capture the Set-Cookie header in Burp HTTP history.
  2. 2. Log in as guest and capture that token as well.
  3. 3. Open a clean browser session and set admin token manually in cookies.
  4. 4. Reload the site and confirm admin access.
Reporting evidence
Include the captured Set-Cookie with the token, the modified cookie value you injected, and screenshots or server responses proving elevated access. Note whether the token expired or was rotated by the server.
Key Takeaway

Server-side token validation and rotation stop cookie-based hijacks; client-side deletion alone is insufficient.

screens.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Privilege Escalation
screens.narratorSegment: Broken access control takes many forms, and understanding the difference between vertical and horizontal privilege escalation is critical. Vertical escalation happens when a lower-privileged user gains access to higher-privileged functionality—for example, a regular user accessing an administrative endpoint such as an admin dashboard by visiting its URL. Horizontal escalation occurs when a user accesses a peer's data at the same privilege level, such as reading another user's documents by changing a file identifier. IDOR is a common mechanism for horizontal escalation when an application exposes raw object identifiers without checking ownership. A useful contrast: vertical escalation often exposes powerful features and configuration changes, while horizontal escalation typically exposes data belonging to other users. From a testing perspective, both require server-side authorization checks. Misconception: assuming that role-based menus or disabled controls enforce authorization. These are purely presentation-layer controls. The correct mitigation is to verify on the server that the authenticated user's role and ownership allow the requested action. In reporting, describe whether the flaw allows read-only exposure, data modification, or privileged operations, because impact and remediation priority differ. Which of these two would you prioritize if an exploit exposed admin functionality?

keyIdea.title: Privilege types
keyIdea.text: Vertical escalation grants higher roles; horizontal escalation exposes peer resources. Both require server-side authorization checks to prevent.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Privilege Escalation

Vertical vs Horizontal Privilege Escalation

Different escalation types imply different impacts and tests.

Vertical Privilege Escalation
A low-privileged user accesses high-privilege functionality, such as admin tools. Test by iterating to known admin endpoints and replaying requests with low-privilege credentials to see if the server enforces role checks.
Impact: configuration changes, user management, or deletion of data.
Horizontal Privilege Escalation / IDOR
A user views or edits another user's data by changing identifiers like user_id or file_id. Test by modifying parameters in captured requests and replaying them to check access control.
Impact: exposure of private user data or unauthorized actions on peers' records.
Pro tip

Always confirm authorization on the server for both role and ownership checks; client-side restrictions are not sufficient.

screens.title: Server-side Authorization Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Preventing broken access control begins with server-side patterns that consistently verify both the user's role and their ownership of a requested resource. A reliable approach maps each resource request to an authorization decision: does the authenticated user's identity and role permit this action on this object? Implement checks centrally where possible—middleware or a shared authorization service—so checks are not forgotten at individual endpoints. Ownership checks are necessary for IDOR protection: the server should resolve the object reference to its owner and deny access when the owner does not match the authenticated user or lacks the required role. Rate limit and logging complement authorization by revealing abuse attempts and blocking rapid enumeration. A common misconception is that role checks alone solve all problems; they do not if ownership is ignored. For example, an application might allow admin-only actions but still use user-supplied file paths for downloads without verifying ownership. When designing fixes, ensure session token validation is combined with authorization checks and that tokens are rotated when privileges change. In a report, recommend a central authorization gate, explicit ownership verification, and fail-safe defaults that deny access unless allowed. What central point in your stack could enforce consistent checks?

keyIdea.title: Authorization design
keyIdea.text: Enforce role and ownership checks on the server through centralized authorization to prevent forgotten or inconsistent checks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Authorization Architecture

Server-side Authorization Patterns

Centralize checks and verify both role and ownership for each request.

Central authorization gate
Implement middleware or a service that receives the authenticated user, requested action, and object identifier, and returns allow or deny. This reduces duplicated logic and missed checks across endpoints.
Ownership verification: resolve the object server-side, check whether the requester is the owner or has an appropriate role, and deny otherwise.
Complement with logging and rate-limiting to detect enumeration or abuse attempts.
Example check
// Pseudocode
if (!authorize(user, action, object)) {
  return 403 // deny by default
}
// proceed with action
Key Takeaway

Authorization must be explicit, server-side, and fail-safe; deny unless a clear allow rule applies.

screens.title: Session Fixation Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Session fixation is an attack where the attacker sets or knows the session identifier that a victim will use, then waits for the victim to authenticate. If the application does not generate a fresh, new session identifier after authentication, the attacker can reuse the fixed session and thereby impersonate the victim. A lab demonstration follows a predictable pattern: the attacker obtains a session ID, persuades the victim to use it—perhaps via a crafted link or injected image—and when the victim logs in, the attacker already holds the valid token. The key defensive measure is rotation: create a new session ID on successful authentication and migrate any necessary session data securely. Another mitigation is binding sessions to additional properties like IP ranges or user agent strings, while being careful not to break legitimate users with dynamic IPs. Misconception: thinking session fixation is the same as session hijacking. They differ: hijacking requires stealing an existing valid token, while fixation requires the server allowing a pre-set token to be used post-login. In a report, show the original token you set, the victim's login, and the fact the token remained valid. How would you confirm rotation is implemented correctly?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Session Fixation

Session Fixation Explained

Attackers set or know a session id and rely on the server keeping it valid after login.

Attack pattern
  • Attacker obtains a session id.
  • Attacker convinces victim to use that id.
  • If the server reuses the id after login, the attacker gains access.
Proof: captured pre-login token and post-login acceptance of that token as valid for the authenticated session.
Mitigation checklist
  • Rotate session ID after successful authentication.
  • Invalidate old sessions on logout.
  • Consider additional session-binding attributes cautiously.
Key Takeaway

A new, unpredictable session id after login prevents an attacker from reusing a pre-set id.

screens.title: DVWA IDOR and Session Exercises
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson ties the chapter's techniques into a single guided lab sequence using DVWA and Burp Suite. Start by setting DVWA security to Low to observe classic vulnerabilities. First, find the IDOR exercise: click to view user profiles and note the URL parameter id=1. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › DVWA Lab

DVWA IDOR and Session Exercises

Follow this controlled sequence to reproduce IDOR and session hijack issues and prepare remediation guidance.

IDOR steps
  1. Set DVWA security to Low and find profile URLs like id=1.
  2. Change id to another value and observe other users' data.
  3. Use Burp Repeater to modify POST body and prove server accepts unauthorized ids.
Session steps
  1. Login as admin, capture Set-Cookie with PHPSESSID in HTTP history.
  2. Login as guest and capture that token too.

Always include captured requests and server responses as evidence and recommend server-side fixes.

screens.title: Effective Mitigations: Authentication, Sessions, Authorization
screens.narratorSegment: Mitigations must be chosen to directly address the observed failure. For broken authentication, adopt long, cryptographically-random reset tokens, enforce reasonable password complexity and rate limiting, and enable multi-factor authentication so a leaked password alone is not enough. For session management, always generate long random session identifiers, set cookies with HttpOnly and Secure flags, rotate session IDs after login, and invalidate sessions at logout and after inactivity. For access control, perform server-side role and ownership checks for each resource and action, centralize authorization logic, and deny by default. Compare these approaches: MFA raises the bar for credential-based attacks but does not replace good session handling; secure cookies protect tokens in transit and from script access but do not prevent an attacker who already has the token; centralized authorization reduces the chance of forgotten checks but must be correctly applied per request. A common misconception is thinking one mitigation solves everything. In practice you must layer defenses: strong authentication, proper session hygiene, and explicit server-side authorization combined make exploitation far more difficult. When reporting, pair findings with the exact mitigation that removes the attack path.

Effective Mitigations: Authentication, Sessions, Authorization

Map defenses to the exact failure mode and use layered controls.

Authentication
MFA, long random reset tokens, rate limiting, and account lockout to stop brute-force and token guessing.
Sessions
Generate secure tokens, set HttpOnly and Secure, rotate on login, and invalidate on logout.
Access Control
Centralize authorization, verify ownership per object, and adopt fail-closed defaults.
Closing note

No single fix is sufficient. Combine strong authentication, session hygiene, and server-side authorization for defense in depth.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These three concepts are central to this chapter. First, Broken Authentication: flaws in how an application verifies user identity. It includes weak passwords, predictable reset tokens, and missing multi-factor authentication; these allow attackers to gain account access and escalate further. Second, Session Management: how a server maintains a user's authenticated state using session tokens. Tokens must be long and random, sent only over HTTPS, and rotated and invalidated appropriately to prevent hijacking and fixation. Third, Broken Access Control: failures to enforce what authenticated users are allowed to do. This includes vertical and horizontal escalation and IDORs where object identifiers are trusted without ownership checks. Remember: these concepts are linked. A compromised credential can lead to a hijacked session, which combined with missing access control checks can expose or modify privileged data. When you write a report, describe which of these concepts the finding falls under and recommend the precise server-side fix that closes the attack path.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we will examine how applications fail to verify identity, maintain session state, and enforce authorization. You will learn what broken authentication means in practice: weak passwords, predictable recovery tokens, and missing multi-factor defenses. We will then explore session weaknesses like hijacking and fixation, where an attacker reuses or forces a session identifier to impersonate a user. Finally, we will study broken access control, including vertical escalation, horizontal escalation, and insecure direct object references. Each idea is tied to concrete testing techniques using tools you already know, such as Burp Suite and simple browser dev tools. Through hands-on steps you will practice changing URL parameters, manipulating cookies, and replaying modified requests to confirm whether the server enforces authorization. Why this matters: authentication and access control are often the gateway to all other vulnerabilities. A single predictable token or an exposed session value can let an attacker reach privileged data or actions. As you proceed, notice common misconceptions: client-side controls are not protections and obfuscation does not equal authorization. Keep an eye out for concrete mitigations we will demonstrate: cryptographically random tokens, HttpOnly and Secure cookies, session rotation, and server-side ownership checks. By the end you should be able to detect these flaws, exploit them in a lab safely, and recommend effective fixes. What is one small change that could stop the simplest attacks you see here?

These objectives guide practical skills you will build. First, you will identify common authentication weaknesses such as weak password policies, predictable reset tokens, and missing multi-factor authentication. That means you will learn to recognize how poor design invites brute-force and credential stuffing. Second, you will understand session management attacks including session hijacking and fixation. You will be able to explain why long, random tokens and cookie flags like HttpOnly and Secure matter. Third, you will explain broken access control categories: vertical and horizontal privilege escalation and IDOR. You will be able to categorize findings and describe the missing server-side checks. Fourth, you will demonstrate exploitation techniques safely in a lab using tools such as Burp Suite, applying Repeater and Intruder to validate flaws. Each objective pairs with a verification milestone so you can show evidence of competency, such as a captured modified request proving an IDOR or a rotated session ID after login. Misconception to avoid: observing a disabled button or hidden link on the client is not proof of authorization. Server-side checks are the ultimate gate. Keep these goals in mind as you follow the hands-on activity and mitigation patterns.

This second objectives slide focuses on tools, testing habits, and common pitfalls. You will learn to use Burp Suite Repeater and Intruder to validate authentication and access control issues safely. That includes intercepting requests, modifying parameters like user identifiers, and replaying altered requests to confirm whether the server grants unauthorized access. Second, you will practice safe lab setup: use DVWA or Juice Shop inside an isolated environment and never test production systems. Third, you will learn to articulate mitigation recommendations: enforce strong, unique reset tokens, enable multi-factor authentication, apply HttpOnly and Secure cookie flags, and rotate session IDs after login. Fourth, you will be able to document findings with proof, such as a modified request showing an IDOR or a cookie change that results in admin access. A common misconception to watch for is assuming obfuscated parameters or client-side checks are secure. The verification milestone is simple: reproduce the flaw in the lab and describe the exact missing server-side validation that allowed it. These objectives ensure you not only find flaws but also explain precise fixes.

Broken authentication means the application does not reliably verify who is trying to access an account or resource. Common examples include weak password policies that accept short or common passwords, insufficient protection against credential stuffing where attackers reuse leaked usernames and passwords, and predictable password reset tokens that can be guessed. A concrete example from a test environment: if password reset links use sequential integers as tokens, an attacker can enumerate or brute-force tokens to reset other users' passwords. Another weakness is informative error messages that reveal whether a username exists, enabling user enumeration. When you test a login form, tools such as Burp Suite Intruder can automate credential lists against the form to confirm weak policies or missing account lockout. A key misconception is believing that client-side validation prevents attacks; it does not. Attackers interact with the server directly. The defending approach includes enforcing long, complex passwords or rate limiting, enabling multi-factor authentication, and using single-use, cryptographically random reset tokens with short expiry. Finally, ensure account lockouts are implemented correctly and cannot be trivially bypassed. Takeaway: authentication must be treated as a critical control point and designed to resist automated and targeted abuse. How would you prove a reset token is predictable in a lab?

Session management is the mechanism that preserves a user's identity across multiple stateless HTTP requests. A server issues a session token after successful authentication and the client presents it on subsequent requests to maintain access. The correct process includes generating a long, cryptographically secure token, setting cookie attributes like HttpOnly and Secure, using SameSite when appropriate, rotating the token on privilege change or login, and invalidating it on logout or timeout. Session hijacking happens when an attacker obtains an existing valid token and reuses it to impersonate the user. Examples include tokens sent over plain HTTP or tokens that are predictable. Session fixation is different: an attacker forces—or convinces—the victim to use a specific token, then waits for the victim to authenticate; if the server does not issue a new token upon authentication, the attacker already owns that session. Misconception: clearing cookies in the browser proves the server invalidated the session; it does not. Always verify server-side invalidation. Practical checks: observe Set-Cookie headers in responses, change the cookie value manually and load the site to confirm access, and verify that tokens change after login. Protect sessions by rotating IDs after login and enforcing short idle timeouts. How would you demonstrate session fixation in a lab?

Insecure Direct Object References, or IDORs, occur when an application uses user-supplied identifiers to access objects without checking whether the requester is authorized. The core test is simple: capture a request where a user views a resource and modify the identifier to another value to see if the server returns a different user's data. A practical walkthrough uses a DVWA-like environment and Burp Suite Repeater. First, find a request that includes a parameter such as id=1. Send it to Repeater. Change id to 2 and resend. If the server returns user two's profile, the server is trusting the parameter without authorization checks. A common misconception is that obfuscating the id on the client prevents access; it does not because an attacker works directly with the HTTP layer. Example evidence includes two response bodies showing different user details for id=1 and id=2. When documenting, capture both requests and responses and note the missing server-side check: there was no ownership or role verification for the requested resource. Mitigation involves server-side mapping from authenticated user to authorized objects and rejecting requests where the requested object is not owned or permitted. How would you show that client-side obfuscation was bypassed?

This lesson guides a controlled lab exercise that demonstrates session hijacking by manipulating a session cookie. The lab uses DVWA with Burp Suite configured as a proxy. First, log in as the admin user and find the login response with Set-Cookie containing PHPSESSID or another session token. Record that token from Burp HTTP history. Next, log out and log in as a different low-privileged user and capture that session token as well. To prove hijack, open a fresh browser profile or clear cookies, then manually set the cookie for the DVWA domain to the admin session value you recorded. Reload the site; if the server accepts that session value, you will be logged in as admin without credentials. This demonstrates why tokens must be resistant to theft and why secure transport and token invalidation matter. Misconception: simply seeing a cookie value in the browser means the server validated its origin; the server must reject forged or expired tokens. Mitigations include sending cookies only over HTTPS, setting HttpOnly to prevent script access, and rotating or invalidating tokens after logout. When you report this finding, include the original captured Set-Cookie header and the reproduction steps so reviewers can confirm the issue reliably.

Broken access control takes many forms, and understanding the difference between vertical and horizontal privilege escalation is critical. Vertical escalation happens when a lower-privileged user gains access to higher-privileged functionality—for example, a regular user accessing an administrative endpoint such as an admin dashboard by visiting its URL. Horizontal escalation occurs when a user accesses a peer's data at the same privilege level, such as reading another user's documents by changing a file identifier. IDOR is a common mechanism for horizontal escalation when an application exposes raw object identifiers without checking ownership. A useful contrast: vertical escalation often exposes powerful features and configuration changes, while horizontal escalation typically exposes data belonging to other users. From a testing perspective, both require server-side authorization checks. Misconception: assuming that role-based menus or disabled controls enforce authorization. These are purely presentation-layer controls. The correct mitigation is to verify on the server that the authenticated user's role and ownership allow the requested action. In reporting, describe whether the flaw allows read-only exposure, data modification, or privileged operations, because impact and remediation priority differ. Which of these two would you prioritize if an exploit exposed admin functionality?

Preventing broken access control begins with server-side patterns that consistently verify both the user's role and their ownership of a requested resource. A reliable approach maps each resource request to an authorization decision: does the authenticated user's identity and role permit this action on this object? Implement checks centrally where possible—middleware or a shared authorization service—so checks are not forgotten at individual endpoints. Ownership checks are necessary for IDOR protection: the server should resolve the object reference to its owner and deny access when the owner does not match the authenticated user or lacks the required role. Rate limit and logging complement authorization by revealing abuse attempts and blocking rapid enumeration. A common misconception is that role checks alone solve all problems; they do not if ownership is ignored. For example, an application might allow admin-only actions but still use user-supplied file paths for downloads without verifying ownership. When designing fixes, ensure session token validation is combined with authorization checks and that tokens are rotated when privileges change. In a report, recommend a central authorization gate, explicit ownership verification, and fail-safe defaults that deny access unless allowed. What central point in your stack could enforce consistent checks?

Session fixation is an attack where the attacker sets or knows the session identifier that a victim will use, then waits for the victim to authenticate. If the application does not generate a fresh, new session identifier after authentication, the attacker can reuse the fixed session and thereby impersonate the victim. A lab demonstration follows a predictable pattern: the attacker obtains a session ID, persuades the victim to use it—perhaps via a crafted link or injected image—and when the victim logs in, the attacker already holds the valid token. The key defensive measure is rotation: create a new session ID on successful authentication and migrate any necessary session data securely. Another mitigation is binding sessions to additional properties like IP ranges or user agent strings, while being careful not to break legitimate users with dynamic IPs. Misconception: thinking session fixation is the same as session hijacking. They differ: hijacking requires stealing an existing valid token, while fixation requires the server allowing a pre-set token to be used post-login.
